title: The fight over Flock and other ALPRs
excerpt: Public pushback against AI-powered camera surveillance has ALPR makers like Flock playing defense.
content_html:
There are over 120,000 of Flock’s automatic license plate reader (ALPR) cameras installed all over the US. Flock’s cameras, and others like them, use AI to identify and track vehicles based on their license plate number, make, model, color, and other info, networked together to track vehicles and people’s movements throughout the day and across the country.

Dozens of communities have canceled contracts for the cameras or turned them off, including Los Angeles, as officials have pushed for more limits on the data they collect, who has access to it, and how it can be used in the future. Earlier this year, Amazon-owned Ring canceled a partnership with Flock after online backlash.

  • Flock CEO: ‘We got this one wrong’

    Image: Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images

    Surveillance tech company Flock is rolling out updates to address reports of cops across the country abusing its tools to stalk ex-romantic partners and others. CEO Garrett Langley is delivering a mea culpa, and in an interview with The Verge, says he’s changed his mind on what responsibility Flock bears for how law enforcement uses it.

    Over the coming weeks, Flock will begin implementing updates that include requiring a previously optional feature called Audit Assistance, which flags “abnormal search behavior” and immediately locks out suspicious users until an administrator reviews their activity. All users will also be required to enter case codes to run searches, ideally limiting the ability to run a query for personal or nefarious purposes. This can be overridden by an administrator for emergency situations, like tracking a missing child, but those will automatically be flagged for review.

    Read Article >

  • Flock cameras? Target practice.

    As BoingBoing notes, a Tennessee candidate for Congress was charged for four counts of felony vandalism for allegedly shooting up Flock cameras. The Blount County sheriff’s office says the suspect admitted to shooting the “ALPR systems” over about a week in July. To say these systems are unpopular is becoming an understatement.

  • Another grim portent for our AI policing future.

    Joel Feder at The Drive reported a frightening story about how Flock cameras, recently suspended by the LAPD, tracked him in Minnesota and sent police after him over “stolen plates.” (They were not.) Flock says its cameras worked “correctly” in the lead-up to a potentially deadly incident. But here we are in our new era of computer policing.

  • The LAPD has suspended its use of Flock’s license plate readers, for now.

    An unnamed spokesperson for Flock told media outlets that unspecified “misconceptions” led to the pause.

  • No, Flock isn’t threatening people for debating surveillance

    Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photos from Getty Images

    On Thursday, the Instagram account for a lecture series in Newport Beach, CA posted a photo of what appeared to be a cease and desist letter from the surveillance technology company Flock Safety. Flock has received significant backlash over its technology and work with law enforcement agencies, and this letter kicked off yet another wave of criticism against the company for allegedly trying to shut down discussions of its work.

    “WE WILL NOT BE SILENCED,” the group, The Saturday Salon, wrote in the Instagram post, which has more than 3,000 likes. A separate post about the letter on Bluesky has more than 360 reposts. The text of the letter demands that the group stop hosting conversations about Flock’s surveillance technology. In a DM from The Saturday Salon’s Instagram account, Schuyler Lifschultz tells The Verge that it “found this letter taped to our front door.”

    Read Article >

  • The all-too-predictable Flock stalking problem.

    A report from 404 Media shows how more than a dozen cases around the US have shown police using Flock to illegally stalk victims. Flock acknowledged it’s aware of 15 incidents, claiming“each surfaced because of the transparency and accountability features deliberately built into our platform.”

    But that doesn’t reflect how some victims only found out by using the HaveIBeenFlocked.com website that Flock has tried to have taken down, or the many years of similar reports with other surveillance tech, a problem the NSA tagged “LOVEINT.”

  • Let’s talk about Ring, lost dogs, and the surveillance state

    Today, let’s talk about the camera company Ring, lost dogs, and the surveillance state.

    You probably saw this ad during the Super Bowl a couple of weekends ago:

    Read Article >

  • Ring’s Flock breakup doesn’t fix its real problem

    Image: The Verge

  • Flock is “pausing further exploration of a potential partnership with Ring.”

    Over the past several months, Flock and Ring explored whether their respective platforms could responsibly complement one another in support of public safety. Throughout those discussions, Flock engaged extensively with customers, public officials, and community stakeholders to understand expectations around accountability, transparency, and lawful use.

    Based on that engagement, Flock and Ring have chosen to cancel the planned integration.

  • Ring cancels its partnership with Flock Safety after surveillance backlash

    Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

    Following intense backlash to its partnership with Flock Safety, a surveillance technology company that works with law enforcement agencies, Ring has announced it is canceling the integration.

    In a statement published on Ring’s blog and provided to The Verge ahead of publication, the company said: “Following a comprehensive review, we determined the planned Flock Safety integration would require significantly more time and resources than anticipated. We therefore made the joint decision to cancel the integration and continue with our current partners … The integration never launched, so no Ring customer videos were ever sent to Flock Safety.”

    Read Article >

  • Dozens of Flock AI camera feeds were just out there

    Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photos from Getty Images

    The livestreams connected to more than 60 of Flock’s AI-powered surveillance cameras were left available to view on the web, allowing someone to see live feeds of each location without needing a username or password, according to findings from tech YouTuber Benn Jordan and 404 Media.

    Flock is a technology company that works with thousands of law enforcement agencies and businesses to deploy a network of AI-powered cameras across the country. It also recently partnered with Ring, giving Flock customers the ability to request footage from users in Ring’s Neighbors app. As noted by 404 Media, many of Flock’s cameras are made to scan a vehicle’s license plates. However, the feeds exposed to the internet connect to Flock’s Condor cameras, which can pan, tilt, and zoom to automatically track people and vehicles.

    Read Article >

  • AI annotators overseas may be reviewing Flock license plate camera footage from the US.

    An exposed dataset from the license plate surveillance company Flock, which is known to work with the US Border Patrol and ICE via local police, showed that some of the AI annotators paid to classify American license plates are located in the Philippines.

    After 404 Media contacted Flock for comment, the dataset disappeared.

  • Amazon’s Ring now works with video surveillance company Flock

    Image: Dan Seifert / The Verge

  • Unprotected license plate surveillance cameras let anyone with a web browser tune in

    Automated license plate recognition systems, also known as ALPR or simply LPR systems, have become increasingly popular — and controversial — tools for law enforcement in recent years. The systems can automatically photograph and record data on license plates in real time, drawing the ire of privacy advocates like those at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which has just released information on security vulnerabilities in ALPR systems across the country.

    “Earlier this year, EFF learned that more than a hundred ALPR cameras were exposed online, often with totally open Web pages accessible by anyone with a browser,” the organization says in the new report released today.

    Read Article >

    On Thursday, the Instagram account for a lecture series in Newport Beach, CA posted a photo of what appeared to be a cease and desist letter from the surveillance technology company Flock Safety. Flock has received significant backlash over its technology and work with law enforcement agencies, and this letter kicked off yet another wave of criticism against the company for allegedly trying to shut down discussions of its work.

    “WE WILL NOT BE SILENCED,” the group, The Saturday Salon, wrote in the Instagram post, which has more than 3,000 likes. A separate post about the letter on Bluesky has more than 360 reposts. The text of the letter demands that the group stop hosting conversations about Flock’s surveillance technology. In a DM from The Saturday Salon’s Instagram account, Schuyler Lifschultz tells The Verge that it “found this letter taped to our front door.”

• The all-too-predictable Flock stalking problem.

    A report from 404 Media shows how more than a dozen cases around the US have shown police using Flock to illegally stalk victims. Flock acknowledged it’s aware of 15 incidents, claiming“each surfaced because of the transparency and accountability features deliberately built into our platform.”

    But that doesn’t reflect how some victims only found out by using the HaveIBeenFlocked.com website that Flock has tried to have taken down, or the many years of similar reports with other surveillance tech, a problem the NSA tagged “LOVEINT.”

• Flock is “pausing further exploration of a potential partnership with Ring.”

    Over the past several months, Flock and Ring explored whether their respective platforms could responsibly complement one another in support of public safety. Throughout those discussions, Flock engaged extensively with customers, public officials, and community stakeholders to understand expectations around accountability, transparency, and lawful use.

    Based on that engagement, Flock and Ring have chosen to cancel the planned integration.

• Ring cancels its partnership with Flock Safety after surveillance backlash

    Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

    Following intense backlash to its partnership with Flock Safety, a surveillance technology company that works with law enforcement agencies, Ring has announced it is canceling the integration.

    In a statement published on Ring’s blog and provided to The Verge ahead of publication, the company said: “Following a comprehensive review, we determined the planned Flock Safety integration would require significantly more time and resources than anticipated. We therefore made the joint decision to cancel the integration and continue with our current partners … The integration never launched, so no Ring customer videos were ever sent to Flock Safety.”

• Dozens of Flock AI camera feeds were just out there

    Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photos from Getty Images

    The livestreams connected to more than 60 of Flock’s AI-powered surveillance cameras were left available to view on the web, allowing someone to see live feeds of each location without needing a username or password, according to findings from tech YouTuber Benn Jordan and 404 Media.

    Flock is a technology company that works with thousands of law enforcement agencies and businesses to deploy a network of AI-powered cameras across the country. It also recently partnered with Ring, giving Flock customers the ability to request footage from users in Ring’s Neighbors app. As noted by 404 Media, many of Flock’s cameras are made to scan a vehicle’s license plates. However, the feeds exposed to the internet connect to Flock’s Condor cameras, which can pan, tilt, and zoom to automatically track people and vehicles.

    Read Article >

blocks.html_en:
• AI annotators overseas may be reviewing Flock license plate camera footage from the US.

    An exposed dataset from the license plate surveillance company Flock, which is known to work with the US Border Patrol and ICE via local police, showed that some of the AI annotators paid to classify American license plates are located in the Philippines.

    After 404 Media contacted Flock for comment, the dataset disappeared.

blocks.html_en:
• Unprotected license plate surveillance cameras let anyone with a web browser tune in

    Automated license plate recognition systems, also known as ALPR or simply LPR systems, have become increasingly popular — and controversial — tools for law enforcement in recent years. The systems can automatically photograph and record data on license plates in real time, drawing the ire of privacy advocates like those at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which has just released information on security vulnerabilities in ALPR systems across the country.

    “Earlier this year, EFF learned that more than a hundred ALPR cameras were exposed online, often with totally open Web pages accessible by anyone with a browser,” the organization says in the new report released today.

content_html_zh:
美国各地安装了超过 120,000 个 Flock 自动车牌读取器 (ALPR) 摄像头。 Flock 的摄像头和其他类似摄像头使用人工智能根据车牌号、品牌、型号、颜色和其他信息来识别和跟踪车辆，并将其联网以跟踪全天和全国范围内的车辆和人员的活动。

包括洛杉矶在内的数十个社区已经取消了摄像机合同或将其关闭，因为官员们对他们收集的数据、谁有权访问这些数据以及未来如何使用这些数据施加了更多限制。 今年早些时候，由于网络强烈反对，亚马逊旗下的 Ring 取消了与 Flock 的合作关系。

  • Flock 首席执行官：“我们搞错了” 图片来源：Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images 监控技术公司 Flock 正在推出更新，以解决全国各地警察滥用其工具跟踪前浪漫伴侣和其他人的报道。 首席执行官加勒特·兰利(Garrett Langley)在接受The Verge采访时表示，他已经改变了对Flock对执法部门如何使用它所承担的责任的看法。在接下来的几周内，Flock将开始实施更新，其中包括要求以前称为“审计协助”的可选功能，该功能会标记“异常搜索行为”并立即锁定可疑用户，直到管理员审查他们的活动。 所有用户还需要输入案例代码才能运行搜索，理想情况下限制了出于个人或恶意目的运行查询的能力。 管理员可以在紧急情况下覆盖此设置，例如跟踪失踪的孩子，但这些会自动标记为供审查。阅读文章 >
  • 群相机？ 目标实践。正如 BoingBoing 指出的那样，一名田纳西州国会候选人因涉嫌射击 Flock 摄像机而被指控犯有四项破坏公物重罪。 布朗特县治安官办公室表示，嫌疑人承认在 7 月份大约一周的时间内射击了“ALPR 系统”。 说这些系统不受欢迎是轻描淡写的。
  • The Drive 的 Joel Feder 报道了一个可怕的故事，讲述了最近被洛杉矶警察局暂停的 Flock 摄像机如何在明尼苏达州追踪他，并因“偷车牌”而派警察追捕他。 （他们不是。） 弗洛克表示，在发生可能致命的事件之前，其摄像机“正常”工作。 但我们正处于计算机警务的新时代。
  • 洛杉矶警察局目前已暂停使用 Flock 的车牌读取器。 Flock 的一位不愿透露姓名的发言人告诉媒体，未具体说明的“误解”导致了暂停。
  • 不，弗洛克并没有因为人们辩论监控而威胁人们 Cath Virginia / The Verge |图片来自 Getty Images 周四，加利福尼亚州纽波特海滩系列讲座的 Instagram 帐户发布了一张看似来自监控技术公司 Flock Safety 的停止信函的照片。 Flock 因其技术和与执法机构的合作而受到强烈反对，这封信引发了对该公司的又一波批评，因为该公司涉嫌试图阻止对其工作的讨论。“我们不会被沉默，”该组织“周六沙龙”在 Instagram 帖子中写道，该帖子获得了 3,000 多个点赞。 Bluesky 上关于这封信的单独帖子已被转发 360 多次。 信中要求该组织停止主持有关 Flock 监控技术的对话。 在《周六沙龙》Instagram 帐户的私信中，Schuyler Lifschultz 告诉 The Verge，它“发现这封信贴在我们的前门上。”阅读文章 >
  • 太可预测的 Flock 跟踪问题。404 Media 的一份报告显示，美国各地发生了十几起警察使用 Flock 非法跟踪受害者的案件。 Flock 承认已发现 15 起事件，并声称“每一起事件的出现都是因为我们平台故意内置了透明度和问责功能。”但这并不能反映出一些受害者是如何通过使用 Flock 试图关闭的 HaveIBeenFlocked.com 网站才发现的，也不能反映出多年来其他监控技术的类似报告，美国国家安全局将这个问题标记为“LOVEINT”。
  • 让我们来谈谈 Ring、丢失的狗和监控状态今天，我们来谈谈摄像头公司 Ring、丢失的狗和监控状态。您可能在几个周末前的超级碗期间看到了这则广告：阅读文章 >
  • Ring 的 Flock 解散并没有解决其真正的问题图片：The Verge
  • Flock 正在“暂停进一步探索与 Ring 的潜在合作伙伴关系。”在过去的几个月里，Flock 和 Ring 探讨了各自的平台是否可以负责任地相互补充，以支持公共安全。 在这些讨论中，Flock 与客户、政府官员和社区利益相关者进行了广泛接触，以了解对问责制、透明度和合法使用的期望。基于这种接触，Flock 和 Ring 选择取消计划中的整合。
  • Ring 因监视强烈反对而取消了与 Flock Safety 的合作关系 图片：Cath Virginia / The Verge、Getty Images 在与执法机构合作的监视技术公司 Flock Safety 的合作遭到强烈反对后，Ring 宣布取消整合。在 Ring 博客上发表并在发布前提供给 The Verge 的一份声明中，该公司表示：“经过全面审查，我们确定计划中的 Flock Safety 整合将需要比预期更多的时间和资源。 因此，我们共同决定取消整合并继续与我们现有的合作伙伴合作…… 该集成从未启动，因此没有任何 Ring 客户视频发送到 Flock Safety。”阅读文章 >
  • 数十个 Flock AI 摄像头源就在那里 Cath Virginia / The Verge |图片来自 Getty Images 根据 YouTube 科技用户 Benn Jordan 和 404 Media 的调查结果，连接到 60 多个 Flock 人工智能监控摄像头的直播可以在网络上查看，无需用户名或密码即可查看每个地点的实时直播。Flock 是一家技术公司，与数千个执法机构和企业合作，在全国范围内部署人工智能摄像头网络。 它最近还与 Ring 合作，让 Flock 客户能够在 Ring 的 Neighbors 应用程序中向用户请求视频片段。 正如 404 Media 所指出的，Flock 的许多摄像头都是用来扫描车辆的车牌的。 然而，暴露在互联网上的信息源连接到 Flock 的 Condor 摄像头，该摄像头可以平移、倾斜和缩放以自动跟踪人员和车辆。阅读文章 >
  • 海外的人工智能注释者可能正在审查来自美国的 Flock 车牌摄像头镜头。车牌监控公司 Flock（已知该公司通过当地警察与美国边境巡逻队和 ICE 合作）曝光的数据集显示，一些付费对美国车牌进行分类的人工智能注释者位于菲律宾。404 Media 联系 Flock 征求意见后，该数据集消失了。
